_link.title: I can explain the relationship between concentration and rate of reaction using collision theory

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the number of particles in a given volume when concentration is increased?
distractors: It decreases
It stays the same
It fluctuates randomly

toLevel2.stem: Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction by increasing:
distractors: the energy of each collision
the activation energy needed
the orientation of particles

toLevel2.stem: A 1.0 mol L⁻¹ solution reacts faster than a 0.1 mol L⁻¹ solution because:
toLevel2.answer: there are more particles per unit volume to collide
distractors: each particle has more kinetic energy at higher concentration
the activation energy is lower at higher concentration
the particles are oriented more correctly at higher concentration

toLevel2.stem: Which statement correctly describes the effect of increasing concentration on reaction rate?
toLevel2.answer: More particles per volume leads to more collisions per second
distractors: Fewer particles per volume leads to faster reactions
The same number of particles collide with more energy
The activation energy is reduced by higher concentration

toLevel2.stem: The relationship between concentration and reaction rate is:
toLevel2.answer: higher concentration leads to a higher rate
distractors: higher concentration leads to a lower rate
concentration has no effect on reaction rate
lower concentration leads to a higher rate

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the concentration of a reactant increases the frequency of collisions between particles.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Increasing concentration increases the kinetic energy of individual reactant particles.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: Increasing concentration increases the number of {{blank:1}} in a given {{blank:2}}, leading to more frequent collisions.
distractors: products
time
catalysts
system

toLevel2.stem: A higher concentration of HCl reacts faster with CaCO₃ because there are more {{blank:1}} ions available to {{blank:2}} with the solid.
distractors: OH⁻
dissolve
Cl⁻
bond

toLevel2.stem: More collisions per unit {{blank:1}} means more opportunities for {{blank:2}} reactions to occur.
distractors: volume
endothermic
mass
catalysed

toLevel3.stem: Why does increasing concentration lead to more collisions per second?
toLevel3.answer: More particles are packed into the same volume, so they meet more often
distractors: Each particle gains more kinetic energy when concentration rises
The activation energy decreases as more particles are present
Particles at higher concentration align in better orientations

toLevel3.stem: How does increased collision frequency lead to a faster reaction rate?
toLevel3.answer: More collisions per second provides more chances for successful collisions
distractors: More frequent collisions reduce the activation energy of the reaction
Each individual collision is more energetic when frequency increases
Frequent collisions improve the orientation of every particle

toLevel3.stem: A student says: 'Higher concentration means each collision is more energetic.' Why is this incorrect?
toLevel3.answer: Concentration affects how often particles collide, not the energy of each collision
distractors: Higher concentration does increase the energy of every collision equally
Concentration only affects whether the system is open or closed
Higher concentration decreases both frequency and energy of collisions

toLevel3.stem: What determines the kinetic energy of particles in a solution?
distractors: The concentration of the solution
The volume of the solution
The type of container used

toLevel3.stem: Why is collision frequency described as a 'key driver' of reaction rate?
toLevel3.answer: Without sufficient collisions, even energetic particles have few chances to react
distractors: Collision frequency is the only factor that determines reaction rate
Collision frequency directly controls the activation energy of the reaction
Without collision frequency, particles cannot have kinetic energy

toLevel3.stem: If the concentration of a reactant is halved, what happens to the collision frequency?
toLevel3.answer: It approximately halves because there are fewer particles per volume
distractors: It doubles because particles have more room to move around
It stays the same because the volume has not changed
It drops to zero because the reaction can no longer proceed

toLevel3.stem: Increasing concentration provides more opportunities for successful collisions by increasing the number of collisions per second.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Concentration affects how {{blank:1}} particles collide, not the {{blank:2}} of each collision.
distractors: hard
frequency
slowly
direction

toLevel3.stem: The kinetic energy of particles in a solution is determined by {{blank:1}}, not by {{blank:2}}.
distractors: concentration
temperature
pressure
volume

toLevel3.stem: Halving the concentration approximately {{blank:1}} the collision frequency because there are {{blank:2}} particles per unit volume.
distractors: doubles
more
triples
larger

toLevel4.stem: A student adds 1.0 mol L⁻¹ HCl to calcium carbonate chips and records the rate. They repeat with 0.5 mol L⁻¹ HCl at the same temperature. What difference would they observe?
toLevel4.answer: The 1.0 mol L⁻¹ reaction is faster due to higher collision frequency
distractors: The 0.5 mol L⁻¹ reaction is faster due to less crowding of particles
Both reactions proceed at the same rate since temperature is constant
The 1.0 mol L⁻¹ reaction is slower due to particles blocking each other

toLevel4.stem: In an industrial process, a chemist doubles the concentration of one reactant while keeping temperature constant. Using collision theory, what changes?
toLevel4.answer: Collision frequency approximately doubles but energy per collision is unchanged
distractors: Both collision frequency and energy per collision approximately double
The activation energy is halved while collision frequency stays the same
Collision energy doubles but collision frequency is unchanged

toLevel4.stem: A student investigates the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. They use five different concentrations. What trend should they expect?
toLevel4.answer: As concentration increases, the time for the reaction decreases
distractors: As concentration increases, the time for the reaction increases
Concentration has no effect on the time taken for the reaction
Only the highest concentration will show any reaction at all

toLevel4.stem: A student explains: 'Diluting the acid slows the reaction because the particles lose energy.' What correction should be made?
toLevel4.answer: Dilution reduces collision frequency, not the energy of individual particles
distractors: The explanation is correct — dilution reduces particle kinetic energy
Dilution actually speeds up the reaction by giving particles more space
Dilution changes the orientation of particles, not their frequency

toLevel4.stem: A reaction between two aqueous solutions is run at 0.2 M and 0.8 M concentrations of one reactant. The 0.8 M trial produces gas four times faster. What collision theory principle explains this?
toLevel4.answer: Four times the particles per volume gives approximately four times the collision frequency
distractors: The 0.8 M solution has four times the kinetic energy per particle
The activation energy is reduced by a factor of four at 0.8 M
The particles are four times better oriented at 0.8 M concentration

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to slow down a reaction that is proceeding too fast. They cannot change the temperature. What should they do?
toLevel4.answer: Dilute the reactant solution to reduce collision frequency
distractors: Add more reactant to increase the activation energy
Seal the container to create a closed system
Stir the mixture to reduce particle collisions

toLevel4.stem: In a titration, 25 mL of 2.0 mol L⁻¹ NaOH is used instead of 25 mL of 0.5 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. How does this affect collision frequency?
toLevel4.answer: Collision frequency increases because there are four times more OH⁻ ions
distractors: Collision frequency decreases because the ions are more crowded
Collision frequency is unchanged because the volume is the same
Collision frequency increases because each ion has more energy

toLevel4.stem: When 1.0 mol L⁻¹ HCl reacts faster than 0.1 mol L⁻¹ HCl with the same solid, it is because there are {{blank:1}} times more H⁺ ions, giving approximately {{blank:2}} times more collisions per second.
distractors: two
two
five
five

toLevel4.stem: Diluting a reactant solution reduces {{blank:1}} frequency because there are fewer particles per unit {{blank:2}}.
distractors: collision
mass
reaction
energy

toLevel4.stem: In an experiment, doubling the concentration of a reactant approximately {{blank:1}} the collision frequency while the {{blank:2}} per collision remains the same.
distractors: halves
frequency
triples
orientation

toLevel5.stem: A reaction rate increases by a factor of three when concentration is tripled, but increases by a factor of ten when temperature is raised by 30°C. What does this comparison reveal?
toLevel5.answer: Temperature has a greater effect because it affects both frequency and energy, not just frequency
distractors: Concentration always has a greater effect on rate than temperature does
Temperature only affects frequency, which is why it has a larger effect
Both factors affect rate equally, and the difference is experimental error

toLevel5.stem: A student concludes: 'Since increasing concentration always increases rate, the highest possible concentration should always be used in industry.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — very high concentrations may be unsafe, costly, or cause unwanted side reactions
distractors: Correct — there is never a disadvantage to using the highest concentration
Incorrect — concentration has no effect on rate in industrial settings
Correct — higher concentration always improves yield and efficiency

toLevel5.stem: As a reaction proceeds, the rate decreases even though temperature is constant. Using collision theory and concentration, explain why.
toLevel5.answer: Reactant concentration decreases over time, reducing collision frequency
distractors: The activation energy increases as the reaction proceeds further
The particles become oriented less favourably as the reaction progresses
The temperature drops because the reaction absorbs all the heat energy

toLevel5.stem: Two reactions at the same temperature have different rates when concentration is doubled. Reaction A shows a rate increase proportional to concentration, while Reaction B shows a rate increase proportional to concentration squared. What can be inferred?
toLevel5.answer: Reaction B involves two particles of that reactant colliding, making it more sensitive to concentration
distractors: Reaction A has no activation energy while Reaction B has a high Ea
Reaction B has lower activation energy so it responds more to concentration
Reaction A is exothermic and Reaction B is endothermic

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims that concentration and gas pressure increase rate by the same mechanism. Is this correct?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — both increase the number of particles per unit volume, increasing collision frequency
distractors: No — concentration increases energy while pressure increases frequency
No — pressure increases orientation while concentration increases frequency
Yes — but only because both factors lower the activation energy

toLevel5.stem: In a reaction where rate = k[A][B], what happens to the rate if [A] is doubled and [B] is halved?
toLevel5.answer: The rate stays the same because the effects cancel out
distractors: The rate doubles because [A] has a larger effect
The rate halves because [B] has a larger effect
The rate quadruples because both changes multiply together

toLevel5.stem: A student writes: 'Adding water to a reaction mixture increases rate because there are more molecules present.' Is this correct?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — adding water dilutes the reactants, decreasing their concentration and collision frequency
distractors: Correct — more molecules in the mixture always increases the reaction rate
Correct — water molecules participate in collisions and increase frequency
Incorrect — adding water increases the activation energy of the reaction

toLevel5.stem: In an excess acid experiment with a fixed mass of solid, the final amount of gas produced is the same at both concentrations, but the initial rate differs. Why?
toLevel5.answer: Both trials have the same limiting reagent, but higher concentration gives a faster initial collision frequency
distractors: The activation energy changes depending on the initial acid concentration used
The solid surface area is different at different acid concentrations
The temperature increases more at higher concentration causing faster rate

distractors: product
energy

toLevel5.stem: Adding water to a reaction mixture {{blank:1}} the concentration of reactants, which {{blank:2}} collision frequency and slows the reaction.
distractors: increases
